strengths: Proposes a clear and useful learned sampler parameterization for diffusion ODEs, combining trainable timestep schedules, additive corrections to theoretically derived multistep coefficients, and access to previous states/velocities.

Empirical results are broad across pixel-space, latent-space, class-conditional, and text-to-image settings, with consistent gains over standard solvers and several learned solver/schedule baselines, especially in low-NFE regimes.

Ablations support the main design choices: the proposed parameterization trains more stably than an S4S-style alternative, and adversarial training improves low-NFE FID and visible artifact quality in several settings.
The paper provides substantial implementation detail in the appendix, including teacher settings, training hyperparameters, memory/time estimates, dataset-size sensitivity, and pseudocode.
The method is practically attractive because inference cost is essentially unchanged relative to the base solver at the same NFE, while training is much cheaper than full student-model distillation.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high: the work combines learned solver coefficients/schedules with a broader multistep parameterization and adversarial loss, but both ingredients are natural extensions of recent LD3/S4S and adversarial diffusion distillation ideas.

The evidence for adversarial training is somewhat uneven. GAS improves low-NFE FID, but at higher NFEs it often matches or slightly worsens GS, and the paper does not deeply analyze when the adversarial term helps or harms fidelity to the teacher.

Evaluation relies heavily on FID. For Stable Diffusion/MS-COCO, FID alone is insufficient because text-image alignment and perceptual preference are central; CLIP score, human preference, or modern T2I benchmarks would make the claims much stronger.

Some baseline comparisons are imperfect: several results are taken from prior papers, some baselines are marked as using different teacher quality, and hardware/training-time comparisons mix H100 and A100 results, making efficiency claims less clean.
The code availability statement appears incomplete in the extracted manuscript, which raises a reproducibility concern despite the detailed appendix.

The method still requires separate optimization for models/datasets/NFE settings, and generalization is only lightly explored on closely related FFHQ/AFHQ transfers; this limits the practical scope compared with training-free solvers.
There is no meaningful discussion of misuse or broader risks of accelerating high-quality generative models, despite the focus on faster image generation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving low-NFE sampling for pretrained diffusion models without retraining the full generator.
The proposed generalized solver parameterization is simple and plausibly useful, with a reasonable initialization from DPM-Solver++ coefficients.
The experiments cover several settings, including pixel-space diffusion, latent diffusion, class-conditional ImageNet, and Stable Diffusion on MS-COCO.
The ablations suggest that the coefficient parameterization improves optimization relative to an S4S-style variant, and that adversarial training can improve low-NFE FID.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental: the method mainly combines learned solver/schedule parameters with a more flexible multistep form and a GAN loss, both well-established ideas in nearby diffusion distillation work.

The evaluation is not fully convincing. Many baselines are copied from prior papers rather than rerun under matched teachers, hardware, data, and implementation details; several comparisons are marked as not directly comparable, yet the paper still makes broad superiority claims.

Some headline claims are overstated. For example, GAS does not consistently outperform all methods across all datasets/NFEs, and in some MS-COCO/ImageNet settings it is comparable to or worse than reported baselines or the teacher.

The reliance on FID alone is weak, especially for adversarially trained samplers and text-to-image generation. There is no CLIP/text alignment metric, precision-recall, diversity analysis, user study, or robust mode-collapse evaluation beyond visual samples and FID.

The adversarial component is under-justified technically. It may improve FID while moving samples away from the teacher, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze the tradeoff between teacher faithfulness, realism, diversity, and prompt fidelity.

The method requires separate optimization for datasets, models, and likely each NFE budget, with backpropagation through the full solver. This limits practical impact despite being framed as lightweight.
Training-time comparisons are not very fair, mixing H100 results for the proposed method with A100/TPU numbers for baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract says code is available but the link is blank, and key implementation details such as discriminator checkpoints and exact baseline reruns are not sufficiently packaged for verification.

The paper would benefit from stronger theory or stability analysis of the learned overparameterized solver; as written, the parameterization appears heuristic and its behavior outside the evaluated settings is unclear.
Presentation has several rough edges, including formatting issues, occasional grammatical errors, and overly strong language relative to the evidence.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: improving very-low-NFE diffusion ODE sampling without training a full student generator, which is highly relevant for resource-constrained deployment.

The Generalized Solver parameterization is simple, well motivated, and appears effective: adding trainable corrections around a theoretically grounded solver is a sensible design that improves optimization stability and convergence.
The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall, covering pixel-space models, latent diffusion, class-conditional ImageNet, and Stable Diffusion text-to-image settings.

Results are strong in the most important low-NFE regimes, with consistent improvements over classical solvers and recent solver/schedule optimization methods such as LD3 and S4S on most reported datasets.
The ablations are useful: the paper separately studies coefficient parameterization, adversarial loss, dataset size, training time, memory, transfer across related datasets, and inference overhead.
The method is practically appealing because it preserves inference-time cost while requiring only lightweight training of solver parameters relative to full diffusion distillation methods.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate rather than transformative: learned solver coefficients, learned timesteps, and adversarially enhanced distillation are all established ideas, and the main contribution is a strong combination and parameterization rather than a fundamentally new sampling principle.

Some comparisons are not fully clean. Several baseline numbers are taken from prior papers, some use different teachers or teacher FIDs, and the S4S latent-space comparison is explicitly marked as not directly fair in some settings.

The Stable Diffusion/MS-COCO evaluation is relatively limited: FID alone is a weak metric for text-to-image quality and prompt alignment, and the reported improvements over the teacher or baselines are modest in several NFE settings.

The adversarial component improves FID, but its behavior is not deeply analyzed beyond aggregate FID and selected samples; stronger diversity, precision/recall, or mode coverage diagnostics would better support the claim that mode collapse is avoided.
The method still requires separate optimization for model/dataset/NFE settings, and the paper only partially addresses generalization of learned solvers across domains or operating points.
Reproducibility is mostly strong in the appendix, but the code availability line in the manuscript appears blank, which weakens the practical reproducibility claim unless corrected.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing diffusion sampling cost by learning solver schedules and coefficients while keeping the pretrained model frozen.

The proposed generalized solver parameterization is simple and well motivated, especially the additive correction around theoretically derived multistep coefficients. The ablations show this design materially improves convergence and FID over less guided parameterizations.
The empirical evaluation is broad, covering pixel-space diffusion, latent diffusion, class-conditional ImageNet, and Stable Diffusion on MS-COCO, with consistent gains in low-NFE regimes.
The adversarial extension is useful in the hardest low-NFE settings and is supported by ablations on GAN loss choice, loss weight, dataset size, and mode-collapse metrics.
The paper includes substantial implementation detail, training-time/memory analysis, and pseudocode, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than transformative: the work combines learned solver coefficients/schedules, theoretical solver initialization, and adversarial loss, all of which are natural extensions of existing solver distillation and adversarial diffusion distillation lines.

Several comparisons are not fully clean. Some baseline numbers are taken from papers, some baselines are reimplemented without official code, teacher configurations differ in places, and training-time comparisons use different GPU types such as H100 vs A100.

The evaluation relies heavily on FID. For text-to-image, there is little assessment of prompt alignment, perceptual preference, CLIP-style metrics, or human evaluation, so the claims about visual quality and detail fidelity are not fully substantiated.

The method requires separate optimization for a target model/dataset/NFE setting, and transfer is only tested between closely related low-resolution datasets. This limits the practical generality of the approach.

The adversarial component improves FID but can move samples farther from the paired teacher under the distillation loss; the paper does not deeply analyze this tradeoff or possible semantic drift, especially for conditional/text-guided generation.
Low-NFE performance at one or two function evaluations remains poor, which narrows the method’s advantage relative to stronger distillation methods in the most latency-constrained setting.

Theoretical understanding is limited: the more flexible solver can be seen as an overparameterized multistep update, but there is little analysis of stability, error behavior, or why the learned coefficients should generalize beyond the training distribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving low-NFE sampling for diffusion ODEs without retraining the full generative model.
The proposed generalized solver parameterization is simple, reasonably well motivated, and practically useful: using additive corrections around a strong base solver is a sensible inductive bias.
The empirical scope is broader than many papers in this area, covering pixel-space models, latent diffusion models, ImageNet, LSUN, and Stable Diffusion/MS-COCO.
The paper includes useful ablations on theoretical coefficient guidance, adversarial loss, adversarial loss type, dataset size, training time, memory, and some mode-collapse diagnostics.
Reported low-NFE FID improvements are sometimes substantial, especially for FFHQ/AFHQv2 and NFE=4 settings.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method is largely a combination of learned solver coefficients/timesteps with an overparameterized multistep form and a standard adversarial loss; the conceptual advance over LD3/S4S and adversarial distillation is incremental.

The evaluation relies heavily on FID and does not convincingly assess perceptual quality, text-image alignment, prompt fidelity, or robustness. This is especially problematic for the Stable Diffusion/MS-COCO experiments, where FID is acknowledged by the authors to be unreliable at higher NFE.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Many baseline numbers are taken from prior papers rather than reproduced under a unified setup, some S4S results are marked as not fairly comparable, and training-time comparisons use different hardware such as H100 versus A100.

The Stable Diffusion setting is weak: the student is trained against an NFE+1 teacher rather than a strong high-NFE teacher, so the method is not clearly distilling the full sampler and the reported gains are small or inconsistent.
The method requires separate optimization for each model, dataset, and target NFE, which limits practical usefulness. The paper acknowledges this but does not resolve it.
The strongest gains are mostly in moderate few-step regimes; performance at NFE=1 and NFE=2 is poor, which weakens the claim of effective extreme acceleration.

The adversarial component introduces extra training complexity and possible distributional risks, but the paper provides only limited diversity checks and no deeper analysis of failure modes, memorization, or sensitivity across prompts/classes.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite detailed hyperparameters: the abstract says code is available but the link appears blank in the manuscript, and several baselines are based on reimplementations or external reported values.
There is little theoretical analysis of stability or consistency of the learned solver, despite framing the contribution as improved ODE discretization.

Overall, the paper is technically plausible and has useful empirical results, but the combination of incremental novelty, fairness concerns in comparisons, limited evaluation metrics, and practical per-setting training cost keeps it slightly below the acceptance threshold for a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: improving very-low-NFE diffusion sampling without retraining the full generative model.
The proposed generalized solver parameterization is simple, well-motivated, and appears to give meaningful gains over fixed solvers and prior solver/schedule optimization methods.
The empirical evaluation is broad, covering pixel-space diffusion, latent diffusion, class-conditional ImageNet, and Stable Diffusion text-to-image settings.

Ablations are reasonably thorough: the paper studies theoretical coefficient guidance, adversarial loss, training dynamics, dataset size, mode collapse indicators, memory, training time, and inference time.
The results are especially strong in low-NFE regimes, where GAS often improves FID substantially over GS and reported baselines while preserving comparable inference speed.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines expanded multistep-solver parameterization, learned schedules, and adversarial loss, all of which are closely related to existing solver distillation and GAN/distillation ideas.
Several key comparisons rely on baseline numbers from prior papers or reimplementations rather than uniformly rerun baselines, which weakens the strength of the empirical claims.

The Stable Diffusion evaluation is less convincing than the other settings: training against an NFE+1 teacher makes the target easier, and FID on MS-COCO alone is insufficient for text-to-image quality and prompt alignment.

The adversarial component improves FID but introduces extra training complexity and hyperparameters; the paper could more clearly separate the contribution of solver parameterization from discriminator training and data effects.
Evaluation is dominated by FID and selected qualitative examples, with limited uncertainty estimates, limited human/preference evaluation, and little discussion of when FID may be misleading.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing from the manuscript alone: code availability appears blank/anonymized, and some implementation choices such as discriminator pretraining, teacher data generation, and baseline tuning materially affect results.
The paper has limited discussion of ethical considerations, failure modes, and risks associated with accelerating large-scale generative models.
